newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebel leader says Mobutu is fleeing.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebel leader says Mobutu is fleeing.

text.p: Rebel leader Laurent Kabila, whose forces occupy a large tract of eastern Zaire, said President Mobutu Sese Seko's return to France on Thursday would leave his routed government army further demoralised.

Mobutu's spokesman said the president, who has spent only three weeks in Zaire since last August, would consult his doctors following treatment for prostate cancer in Switzerland last year. But Kabila said he was simply fleeing Zaire.

"Those soldiers who still supported Mobutu expected that his presence would turn the tide against us, and now they can see he is fleeing the country they will be even more demoralised," Kabila told Reuters.
"While he goes off to France all Mobutu has left with his people are foreign mercenaries."
Kabila said his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) was preparing to meet a government counter-offensive promised by Mobutu.
Kabila's rebels occupy a 600-km (400-mile) stretch of eastern Zaire bordering Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi. Their stated goal is to take Kinshasa and end Mobutu's 31-year-long reign.

Ill-disciplined and largely unpaid government forces have fled and looted several major towns since the rebellion erupted in October. Over half a million Hutu refugees in border camps returned to Rwanda during the fighting.
Mobutu spent less than a month in Zaire on his return from Switzerland and the French Riviera on December 17 but during that time he reshuffled his government and army high command.
The rebels accuse him of assembling an army of foreign mercenaries to mount the long-promised counter-attack.

A Zairean opposition party, the Union for Democracy and Social Progress, said in Brussels on Thursday that some 300 mercenaries paid by France were in Zaire to support Mobutu's government and 700 others had been recruited. A spokeswoman said the mercenaries were from France, Belgium and South Africa.
The Paris daily Le Monde carried a similar report on Tuesday.
Zaireans in the rebel-held east had mixed views on Mobutu's departure.
"We are afraid it may mean he has now prepared a counter- offensive and is happy to sit back and watch it from France," said teacher Gerald Serufuli.
"We hope it is a sign that he is unable to do anything more and has given up on the war," said mechanic Pierre Ntalemura.

There is growing insecurity in the region as Kabila's forces try to track down groups of village warriors who were once allies but have turned against them, as well as remnants of the former Rwandan army and militia groups.

"We have a little bit of trouble from the Interahamwe (Rwandan Hutu militia) who we chased from Walikale and who are now attacking us to try to find a safe road to somewhere they can be helped by friends like Mobutu and the French," Kabila said.

Much of the former Rwandan army, which took refuge in Zairean camps after being defeated in the civil war that followed the 1994 genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis, was driven deeper into Zaire by the rebels.

Kabila said the groups of Rwandans driven from Walikale, 130 km (85 miles) west of the border town of Goma, had been crossing the Masisi region 60 km (40 miles) away and heading into the thick forests that approach the Rwandan border.
Kabila's rebels, many of them Tutsis, are backed by Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated government.
